newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan's king appeals for peace talks revival.
newsitem.headline: Jordan's king appeals for peace talks revival.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein vowed on Saturday to continue a flurry of diplomatic activity to help restore calm in the West Bank and Gaza on the fourth day of clashes between Israeli troops and Palestinians.
King Hussein, speaking to reporters after chairing a council of ministers meeting, appealed for a revival of Arab-Israeli peace talks on all tracks.
Fifty-four Palestinians and 14 Israeli soldiers have been killed in the clashes sparked by Israel's opening this week of a tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Arab East Jerusalem

The king said that Jordan, the legal custodian of holy Moslem sites in Arab East Jerusalem since 1950, will continue to care for them until final talks on the status of the disputed city to avoid a legal vacuum that Israel could use to control the shrines.

The permanent status talks, the final stage of the 1993 self-rule accord between Israel and the PLO, began in May but stalled after the election of Israel's hardline Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that month.

"Jordan is continuing contacts with all concerned parties," he said, referring to several telephone contacts he had in the past 48 hours with Netanyahu, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat, Saudi and Egyptian leaders and the ambassadors of Britain, the United States and Israel in Amman.

"I hope their (the envoy's) countries will carry out the role that should be achieved at this stage in attracting world attention to what is going on," he added. "And we will continue these efforts with all our means and capabilities".
The king said Jordan would "soon prepare a document on the overall situation that could be used as a basis in the future to tackle this issue".
Amman continues to pay salaries for the upkeep of the Moslem shrines, its clerics, restoration work and runs Sharia courts in Arab Jerusalem -- a thorny issue in Jordanian-PLO ties.

And Jordan's 1994 peace treaty with Israel recognised Amman's "special role" over Moslem holy shrines in Arab Jerusalem, which Palestinians hope will be the capital of their future state, an idea vehmently opposed by Israel.
The king said he instructed Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti to boost coordination with the Palestinian Authority running self-rule in parts of the West Bank and the Gaza Strip.
Ties between the king and Arafat, who heads the authority, have long been marred by historic rivalry over who represents Palestinians, who make up many of Jordan's 4.2 million people.
